t1.title: Notify the recipient of a new secure message
t1.requirement:
When a practitioner sends a secure message (`POST /api/messages`), the recipient must be told that a message is waiting.

- Send the recipient one email (to the email address on their user account) and one push notification to each device they registered (`devices` table).
- The email and the push only say that a new secure message is waiting and that they need to sign in to read it. Include the portal address (`APP_BASE_URL`) in the email.
- The message subject and body, the patient's name and the reason for care are PHI: none of them may appear in the email or the push notification (subject line, body, title or data).
- A notification failure must not make the message send fail: the message is stored and the API still answers 201.

t2.title: Let the recipient read a message
t2.requirement:
Add `GET /api/messages/{id}` so the signed-in recipient can open a message from their inbox.

- Only the recipient of the message may read it. Anyone else (another user, any other role including admins, any user of another practice) gets a 404, so the response does not reveal that the message exists.
- Unauthenticated requests get 401.
- The 200 response is exactly `{ "id", "subject", "body", "sentAt", "from": { "name" } }` where `from.name` is the sender's display name. Return no other field.
- Opening the message as the recipient marks it as read (`read_at`).

A first engagement is defined by what goes in and what comes out, not by a duration.

  • From your team: one task where Claude Code fails and one where it succeeds, the instruction files and settings it actually loads, what a good result looks like, and the traces of those runs. No patient data is needed at any point.
  • A diagnosis that can conclude missing context, permissions, tests that do not catch the failure, a task that is too broad, or instructions that are badly put together, and says which, with the run that shows it.
  • The changes themselves: each rule tied to the failure it fixes, and anything that must never happen written as a test or a hook.
  • A simple way for your team to replay the checks whenever the files change.

In our own rule files, each rule is one or two sentences tied to a failure we actually saw, and it comes out when the model stops making that mistake; anything that must never happen moves out of prose into a test or a hook.

Versioned rules, deterministic blocks and replayable logs also give a security review something concrete to read: which rule changed, what a hook refused, and the run that shows it.
